This supplement contains additional methods, results and discussion as well as one table, four supplementary figures and associated references.

## Supplemental Methods

Several morphological variables were collinear and we chose *a priori* to include surface area as a predictor while omitting all other morphological variables with a VIF > 3 including dynamic ratio and shoreline complexity, and the inclusion of any of these three did not qualitatively change the analysis results (**Table Sx**). We also excluded circularity as a predictor, despite its relatively low VIF value, given counterintuitive relationships where partial dependence plots showed emissions increasing with circularity. We expect this prediction was likely due to the negative relationship between circularity and surface area (pearson correlation coefficient = 0.5; smaller reservoirs are more round), as has been reported elsewhere [@casas_ruiz_2021].

## Supplemental Results and Discussion

### Relative drainage area

Relative drainage area (RDA), calculated as the ratio of watershed to reservoir surface area, serves as a proxy for the per-unit-area loading rate of watershed derived sediment into a reservoir (i.e., g sediment m^-2^ d^-1^) and has been shown to correlate with reservoir CH~4~ emission rates [@beaulieu_et_al_2020]. RDA was identified as the fourth and sixth most important predictor in the national models of CH~4~ total and diffusion, respectively, but was not selected as an important variable in any of the local models, possibly because the local models also include measurements of percent sediment carbon (third most important predictor in the total and diffusive local models) which may serve as a stronger index of carbon availability than RDA.

### Buoyancy frequency

Center buoyancy frequency, an index of the strength of thermal stratification, was the fourth best predictor of CH~4~ diffusion in the local RF model. CH~4~ diffusion rates showed a positive non-linear relationship with reservoir buoyancy frequency, with mean predicted emissions increasingly steeply from un-stratified systems to weakly stratified ones (with a threshold at 0.0006 s^-1^) and then remaining relatively flat as stratification increased **(Figure S2)**. An analysis of mixing regimes across 34 ponds and shallow lakes found that a threshold density gradient of 0.287 kg m^-3^ m^-1^ distinguished conditions promoting mixing from stable stratified conditions [@holgerson_2022]. Assuming freshwater at 10 degrees C, this would roughly correspond to a center buoyancy frequency of 0.002 s^-1^, which is nearly an order of magnitude higher than the threshold we observed here. Thus, we report the lowest rates of CH~4~ diffusion from systems that are very well mixed. Such conditions would be less likely to support a build-up of methane in the water column because oxygen can efficiently mix down to the sediment water interface. Several studies have examined the relationship between center buoyancy frequency and CH~4~ concentrations, but have ultimately found bottom water dissolved oxygen as a more important predictor of surface emissions [@webb_2019], or found that higher buoyancy frequencies resulted in higher deep water CH~4~ concentrations without resulting in measurable differences at the surface [@rimas_2026]. One study found that buoyancy frequency was negatively related to CH~4~ concentrations in reservoirs (but at higher buoyancy frequencies-- mean of 0.011 s^-1^ and standard deviation of 0.01), but positively related to CH~4~ concentrations in wetlands [@jensen_2023]. In this study, buoyancy frequency may be a better predictor than bottom dissolved oxygen concentrations (which were measured at every site) because it may integrate over a longer timescale than the dissolved oxygen signal.

## Harsha Lake emission driver maps

Spatially explicit maps of several drivers of the CH~4~ total emission rate random forest model were constructed for William H Harsha lake in southwest Ohio (lake_id == 1031 in dataset). These spatially explicit datasets were subsequently used to inform predictions of the total CH~4~ emission rate at the lake.

Map of water depth (A), chlorophyll-*a* (B), water temperature near sediment-water interface (C), water temperature 0.1 m below water surface (D), turbidity 0.1 m below water surface (E), and sediment organic carbon (F) in William H.
